concepts.name: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment & Removal
key_dimensions: Constitutional provisions under Article 324: multi-member vs single-member ECI and historical evolution

Appointment process post Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 vs. pre-2023 convention — UPSC trap on who appoints
Removal asymmetry: CEC removed like SC judge (Article 324(5)), other ECs can be removed on CEC's recommendation — a classic 'only' clause trap
Autonomy concerns: salary charged to Consolidated Fund vs. voted expenditure distinction

concepts.name: Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Legal Status, Scope & Enforcement
key_dimensions: MCC has no statutory backing — operates on moral/conventional authority; contrast with statutory provisions of RPA 1951
Trigger point: MCC comes into force on date of election announcement, not date of notification — common UPSC trap
Applicability to incumbent government: restrictions on policy announcements, use of government machinery
ECI's enforcement powers under Article 324 vs. specific MCC provisions; recent controversies on selective enforcement

concepts.name: Delimitation: Process, Authority & Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: Constitutional basis: Articles 82 (Lok Sabha) and 170 (State Assemblies) — delimitation after every census
Delimitation Commission Act and composition of Delimitation Commission; finality of orders (not subject to court scrutiny — Article 329(a))
Freeze on delimitation: 84th Amendment froze seat allocation until 2026 census; 87th Amendment readjusted constituencies based on 2001 census without increasing seats
SC/ST reservation of seats in delimitation: rotation principle and its implications; difference between reserved seats and reserved constituencies

concepts.name: Voter Eligibility & Electoral Roll: Registration and Exclusions
key_dimensions: Article 326: Universal Adult Suffrage — minimum age 18 (lowered from 21 by 61st Amendment, 1988)
Grounds for disqualification from electoral roll: non-citizenship, unsound mind (declared by court), corrupt/illegal practice, imprisonment — Article 326 exclusions
Service voters, overseas voters (NRI voting rights under RPA amendment 2010) — eligibility nuances
Electoral Registration Officers' role; Form 6, 7, 8 — additions, deletions, corrections; EPIC vs. Aadhaar linkage controversy

concepts.name: Disqualification of Candidates: RPA 1951 vs. Tenth Schedule vs. Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: Article 102 & 191 disqualifications for Parliament and State Legislature: office of profit, unsound mind, insolvent, non-citizenship, disqualified by law
Section 8 RPA 1951: conviction-based disqualification — 2-year imprisonment threshold; Lily Thomas case (2013) striking down Section 8(4) protection for sitting members
Office of Profit: no statutory definition, Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act exemptions — a major UPSC trap area
Anti-defection (Tenth Schedule) disqualification: decided by Speaker/Chairman (not ECI) — critical distinction from other disqualifications

concepts.name: Election Schedule: Notification, Nomination, Withdrawal & Polling Dates
key_dimensions: Statutory timeline under RPA 1951: notification → last date of nomination (minimum 7 days) → scrutiny → withdrawal (2 days after scrutiny) → polling (minimum 14 days after last withdrawal) — exact day counts are UPSC traps
Role of Returning Officer vs. Election Commission in scheduling; who issues notification (President for LS, Governor for State)
By-elections: must be held within 6 months of vacancy (with exceptions) — Section 151A RPA
Simultaneous elections debate: constitutional amendments required (Articles 83, 85, 172, 174, 356)

concepts.name: Electronic Voting Machines (EVM): Legal Status, Challenges & VVPAT
key_dimensions: Legal backing: Section 61A RPA 1951 (inserted 1989) enables use of voting machines; not mentioned in Constitution directly
VVPAT: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail — introduced 2013; Supreme Court rulings on VVPAT slip verification percentage (2019 judgment limiting to 5 EVMs per constituency)
Challenges to EVM tampering: ECI's technical expert committee responses; 'totalizer' demand and its current status
Comparison with ballot paper system; countries that reverted from EVMs — context for UPSC essay/GS questions

concepts.name: Election Symbols: Allotment, Freezing & Disputes
key_dimensions: Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 — quasi-judicial order under Article 324, not a statute
Recognized national vs. state party criteria: vote share (6% + 4 seats for national; 6% + 2 seats for state) or seat criteria — exact thresholds are UPSC traps
Symbol freezing in party splits: ECI's power to decide which faction gets the symbol (Sadiq Ali case 1972, Shinde vs. Thackeray 2022 controversy)
Free symbols for independents; reserved symbols exclusively for recognized parties — distinction and implications

concepts.name: Election Expenses: Limits, Disclosure & Enforcement
key_dimensions: Section 77 RPA 1951: candidates must maintain election expense accounts; current Lok Sabha limit (~₹95 lakh) vs. Assembly (~₹40 lakh) — note: party expenditure not subject to same limits
Section 10A: disqualification for 3 years for failure to lodge election expense account — not same as corrupt practice disqualification
Surrogate expenditure and star campaigners: expenses of star campaigners NOT counted in candidate's account (only 3 star campaigners' expenses counted if party has fewer than 3 candidates in state)
Electoral Bonds Scheme: Supreme Court striking it down (Feb 2024) — anonymity vs. transparency tension; contrast with declared donations

concepts.name: Corrupt Practices & Electoral Offences under RPA 1951
key_dimensions: Section 123 RPA: 8 corrupt practices — bribery, undue influence, appeal on grounds of religion/race/caste/community/language, use of government machinery, publication of false statements, illegal gratification, incurring excessive expenditure, booth capturing
Distinction between corrupt practice (Section 123) and electoral offence (Section 125-136) — corrupt practice leads to election being void; electoral offence leads to criminal punishment
Booth capturing (Section 58A): election can be countermanded or adjourned by ECI — suo motu power
Section 8A: disqualification for corrupt practice — decided by President on ECI's opinion (not automatic); duration up to 6 years beyond imprisonment

concepts.name: Election Petition: Jurisdiction, Grounds & Limitations
key_dimensions: Article 329(b): election disputes cannot be raised except by election petition; ordinary civil courts have no jurisdiction — absolute bar
Jurisdiction: High Court for Parliament and State Legislature elections (Section 80A RPA); Supreme Court only in appeal — NOT in original jurisdiction
Grounds for declaring election void (Section 100) vs. grounds for declaring petitioner elected (Section 101) — distinction is a UPSC trap
Limitation period: 45 days from date of election of returned candidate; who can file — any elector or defeated candidate (not just candidates)

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law: Tenth Schedule — Triggers, Exceptions & Decision Authority
key_dimensions: Grounds for disqualification: voluntarily giving up party membership OR voting/abstaining contrary to party whip without prior permission and condoning within 15 days
Exceptions: merger (requires 2/3rd of legislative party — not original party) — pre-1985 'split' provision of 1/3rd was deleted by 91st Amendment 2003
Decision authority: Speaker/Chairman — NOT ECI, NOT President/Governor; Kihoto Hollohan case (1992): Speaker's decision subject to judicial review but only after final order
Nominated members: can join a party within 6 months of nomination — after that, subject to anti-defection; independent members cannot join any party after election

concepts.name: President & Vice-President Elections: Method, Electorate & Disputes
key_dimensions: Presidential election (Article 54-55): Electoral College = elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of all State Legislative Assemblies + elected members of UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K) — nominated members excluded (UPSC classic trap)
Single Transferable Vote with proportional representation; value of votes of MLAs varies by state population; MP votes are uniform — formula under Article 55(2)
Vice-President election (Article 66): elected by members of BOTH Houses in joint sitting — NOT state legislatures; only elected + nominated members of Parliament vote (contrast with President)
Disputes: Presidential election disputes go to Supreme Court (Article 71); VP election disputes also to Supreme Court — no parallel in High Court

concepts.name: Speaker & Deputy Speaker Elections: Process, Removal & Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: Articles 93 (LS) and 178 (State Assembly): Speaker and Deputy Speaker elected by House members from among themselves — no external authority involved
Removal: 14 days' notice required; resolution passed by effective majority (not special majority) — but Speaker can vote in case of tie (casting vote)
Speaker's role during dissolution: Speaker continues until newly elected House meets (unlike the House itself); Deputy Speaker acts when Speaker's office is vacant
Anti-defection adjudication by Speaker: conflict of interest issue — Supreme Court in Nabam Rebia case (2016) held that Speaker facing removal notice cannot decide disqualification petitions

concepts.name: Rajya Sabha Elections: Method, Representation Principle & Open Ballot
key_dimensions: Article 80: Rajya Sabha — states represented on basis of population (not equal representation unlike US Senate); 4th Schedule lists seats for each state
Election method: Single Transferable Vote by proportional representation; elected by elected members of State Legislative Assembly only (not Legislative Council)

Open ballot system (2003 amendment to Election Conduct Rules): voter must show ballot to party agent before depositing — prevents cross-voting while maintaining secrecy from ECI; constitutional validity upheld
Quota formula for RS elections: Total valid votes ÷ (Seats + 1) + 1; Presidential nomination of 12 members (Art. 80(3)) — nominated members cannot vote in Presidential election (trap)

concepts.name: NOTA (None of the Above): Legal Basis, Effect & Limitations
key_dimensions: Origin: Supreme Court direction in PUCL vs. Union of India (2013) — not a statutory provision but rule-based under Conduct of Election Rules 1961
NOTA has no electoral value: candidate with maximum votes wins even if NOTA gets more votes than winner — NOTA is not a 'negative vote' that can cancel election (common misconception)
ECI's 2018 order for local body elections: if NOTA gets majority, re-election to be held — but this applies only to some state election commissions, NOT general elections
Distinction between NOTA and right to reject: NOTA exists, statutory right to reject (re-election if NOTA wins) does not exist at Parliamentary/Assembly level

concepts.name: State Election Commission vs. Election Commission of India: Powers, Jurisdiction & Autonomy
key_dimensions: Article 243K (Panchayats) and 243ZA (Municipalities): State Election Commission superintends, directs, controls elections to PRIs and ULBs — NOT ECI's jurisdiction (UPSC classic confusion trap)
SEC: appointed by Governor; removed like HC judge (not like CEC); service conditions cannot be varied to disadvantage after appointment
Power overlap issue: ECI can notify election schedule for State Assembly coinciding with PRI elections — SEC and ECI operate independently; MCC applies only to ECI-conducted elections
K. Krishnamurthy vs. Union of India (2010): SC clarified distinction; recent controversies on SEC autonomy in states (Tamil Nadu, West Bengal SEC appointment disputes)

concepts.name: Electoral Reforms: Key Recommendations & Legislative Changes
key_dimensions: Major committees: Tarkunde Committee (1974), Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) on state funding of elections, Law Commission 170th Report (1999) — recommendations status (implemented vs. pending)
Implemented reforms: lowering voting age (1988), EVM introduction, NOTA, VVPAT, Electoral Bond (struck down 2024), deletion of Section 8(4) by Supreme Court
Pending reforms: state funding of elections, simultaneous elections (Kovind Committee 2024 report), inner-party democracy, criminalization of politics (179th Law Commission Report)
Section 33B RPA (struck down): attempted to shield electoral bond donors from disclosure — Assn. for Democratic Reforms case 2024 (Supreme Court 5-judge bench unanimous ruling)

concepts.name: Conduct of Elections Rules 1961: Key Provisions & Procedural Traps
key_dimensions: Statutory basis: made under Section 169 RPA 1951 — these rules govern actual conduct (ballot design, counting, EVMs) as distinguished from RPA which governs qualification/disqualification
Rule 49O (now replaced): elector's right not to vote — was an administrative provision, NOT constitutional right; often confused with NOTA

Counting rules: postal ballots counted first; declaration of result only after all valid votes counted; Rule 63 — returning officer's decision on validity of votes is final subject to election petition
Secrecy of voting: Rule 39B prohibits exhibiting marked ballot; open ballot exception only for RS/MLC elections — knowing this distinction prevents errors in exam

concepts.name: Criminalization of Politics: Legal Framework, Judicial Interventions & Disclosure Requirements
key_dimensions: Section 8 RPA 1951: disqualification only on conviction with 2+ years imprisonment — mere charge-sheeting or FIR not sufficient (common misconception in prelims)
Supreme Court directions: Public Interest Foundation vs. UOI (2019) — candidates with criminal cases must publish in newspapers and on party website; parties must explain why such candidates selected

Association for Democratic Reforms case series: right to information of voters elevated to fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a); affidavit disclosure of criminal antecedents, assets, liabilities mandatory
Proposed reforms: disqualification on framing of charges (Law Commission recommendation) vs. conviction-based (current law) — constitutional implications of each approach under Article 14
